Recent work supports intervention-based diagnosis: [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations; [FCESR (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13632) distinguishes sufficiency—retained interactions preserve a recommendation—from necessity—removed interactions overturn it. [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential) includes inference-time shuffling of histories for already-trained GRU4Rec models, directly relevant to frozen-model order probes.

Suggested adaptation: keep each user’s target and candidate set fixed; compare intact history against prefix removal, recent-item removal, equal-sized random removal, and shuffling that preserves the final item. Report paired target-rank changes, target-versus-negative margin changes, and HR@10 gains/losses, stratified by history length. Compact retained interactions and restore left padding; read the final nonpadding state. Prefix-removal damage with the recent suffix preserved supports useful older context; recent-removal damage measures dependence on recent evidence. Neither establishes excessive recency or stale intent without evidence of predictive harm.

[TimeSHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00073) supplies an earlier recurrent-model foundation for timestep attribution and prefix pruning. As complementary diagnostics, measure target-margin gradients with respect to input embeddings and recurrent states by lag, then test whether highly attributed events cause larger deletion effects than random events. Hidden-state displacement alone need not imply ranking relevance. [Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/8160-sanity-checks-for-saliency-maps.pdf) motivates parameter-randomization controls on disposable diagnostic copies. Keep one frozen trained GRU4Rec per category; distinguish local sensitivity, perturbation artifacts, and predictive usefulness from causal claims about user intent.
